payload.name: log-frequency-spectrogram
payload.scope: A human-made time-frequency representation that maps a signal's frequency axis to a logarithmic (or other perceptual) scale so that bins are spaced proportionally to their center frequency. It persists through audio analysis libraries and research implementations that compute the representation from a signal's short-time Fourier transform with frequency-axis resampling.

definition.body: A log-frequency spectrogram is a human-made time-frequency representation that maps a signal's spectrum onto a frequency axis whose spacing is proportional to the logarithm of frequency. Its parameters are: (1) the frequency mapping function (logarithmic with a specified base, Mel scale, or equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth scale), (2) the number of frequency bins per octave or decade, (3) the reference frequency and lowest frequency, and (4) the windowing function and hop size used in the underlying short-time Fourier transform. It persists as a computed array in audio analysis libraries (librosa, Essentia, MIRtoolbox) and research code that transforms linear-frequency spectrograms via frequency-axis interpolation. e.g.: librosa.logspec function output; Essentia LogFrequencySpectrum algorithm output; MIRtoolbox logspec function; constant-Q transform spectrogram display | not: constant-q-transform (the algorithm that computes it); linear-frequency spectrogram (frequency axis spaced uniformly in Hz) [formal: specrogramm frequency logarithmica | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: constant-q-transform-derived
payload.scope: A human-made class of time-frequency representations that inherit the constant-Q property from the constant-Q transform — frequency bin bandwidth proportional to center frequency — while differing from the canonical CQT in discretization, window shape, or computational structure. Built for practical audio analysis where the ideal CQT's continuous formulation must be adapted for digital implementation.

definition.body: A constant-Q transform-derived representation is a human-made time-frequency representation that maintains the constant-Q property (bin bandwidth proportional to center frequency) while differing from the canonical constant-Q transform in at least one of: discretization scheme, analysis window shape, or computational structure. Its parameters are: (1) the discretization method (oversampled DFT on geometric frequency grid, filter bank implementation, or zero-padded FFT), (2) the analysis window (Gaussian, Kaiser-Bessel derived, or other constant-Q-preserving window), (3) the quality factor Q and its constancy across frequency, and (4) the overlap and phase treatment. It persists as implementations in audio analysis libraries and research code where the idealized continuous CQT must be adapted for discrete computation. e.g.: librosa.cqt implementation; Essentia ConstantQBands algorithm; Scikit-learn's constant-Q feature extraction; OpenL3 audio embeddings use CQT-derived representation | not: constant-q-transform (the idealized continuous formulation); log-frequency-spectrogram (broader class including non-constant-Q log scaling) [formal: transformatio constantis-Q derivata | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: linear-prediction-coefficient
payload.scope: A human-made set of scalar coefficients that parameterize a linear prediction model for a signal, quantifying how each sample can be estimated as a weighted sum of previous samples. These coefficients form the core representation in speech coding, speaker identification, and spectral analysis.

definition.body: A linear prediction coefficient is a human-made scalar parameter a_k that appears in a linear prediction model where a signal sample x[n] is estimated as a weighted sum of P previous samples: x_hat[n] = sum_{k=1}^{P} a_k x[n-k]. Its parameters are: (1) the prediction order P, determining the number of coefficients, (2) the coefficient values themselves a_1 through a_P, computed via autocorrelation, covariance, or lattice methods, and (3) the normalization convention (whether a_0 = 1 or the coefficients are normalized). It persists through speech coding standards (G.729, ACELP codecs), LPC analysis software (MATLAB lpc, librosa.lpc), and academic implementations across signal processing. e.g.: MATLAB lpc() function output; G.729 CELP codec LSP parameters derived from LPC coefficients; librosa.lpc function output; ITU-T G.721 ADPCM quantizer uses related coefficients | not: linear-prediction-filter (the filter whose transfer function is the reciprocal of the prediction polynomial); reflection-coefficient (parcor coefficients, which are a nonlinear reparameterization of LPC coefficients) [formal: coefficient praedictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: line-spectral-pair
payload.scope: A human-made pair of spectral representations derived from linear prediction coefficients that provide a robust parameterization for speech coding, mapping the LPC polynomial roots to frequencies and line spectral frequencies for stable quantization.

definition.body: A line spectral pair is a human-made pair of spectral representations (line spectral frequencies and line spectral amplitudes) derived from the roots of the LPC prediction polynomial's even and odd parts. Its parameters are: (1) the number of LSP frequencies (typically equal to the LPC prediction order P), (2) their values in radians or normalized frequency, ordered increasingly between 0 and pi, and (3) the quantization scheme used for transmission. It persists through speech coding standards (G.729, AMR, GSM-EFR) that use LSPs instead of raw LPC coefficients for stable interpolation and quantization. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 LSP parameter encoding; AMR codec LSP-to-LPC conversion; GSM-EFR LSP vector quantization; ACELP codebook search uses LSP interpolation | not: linear-prediction-coefficient (raw LPC coefficients, unstable for quantization); line-spectral-frequencies (LSF only, not the full pair including amplitudes) [formal: pares lineares spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: linear-prediction-filter
payload.scope: A human-made all-pole digital filter whose transfer function is the reciprocal of a linear prediction error polynomial, used to synthesize speech or model resonant structures from linear prediction coefficients. It represents the vocal tract or other resonant systems in speech coding.

definition.body: A linear prediction filter is a human-made all-pole digital filter with transfer function H(z) = G / A(z) where G is a gain factor and A(z) = 1 + sum_{k=1}^{P} a_k z^(-k) is the prediction error polynomial. Its parameters are: (1) the prediction coefficients a_k (LPC coefficients), (2) the gain G (scale factor for input excitation), (3) the prediction order P (equal to the number of poles), and (4) the input excitation signal (pulse train for voiced, white noise for unvoiced). It persists as the synthesis filter in speech coding standards (G.729 CELP, AMR), LPC vocoders (AMDF vocoder, Klatt synthesizer), and speech analysis software. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 CELP synthesis filter; Klatt synthesizer all-pole vocoder; MATLAB lfilter with LPC coefficients; librosa lpc synthesis in speech processing | not: prediction-error-filter (the FIR analysis filter with transfer function A(z), not G/A(z)); linear-prediction-coefficient (the scalar parameters a_k, not the filter itself) [formal: filter praedictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

Its parameters are: (1) the prediction coefficients a_k (LPC coefficients), (2) the gain G (scale factor for input excitation), (3) the prediction order P (equal to the number of poles), and (4) the input excitation signal (pulse train for voiced, white noise for unvoiced). It persists as the synthesis filter in speech coding standards (G.729 CELP, AMR), LPC vocoders (AMDF vocoder, Klatt synthesizer), and speech analysis software. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 CELP synthesis filter; Klatt synthesizer all-pole vocoder; MATLAB lfilter with LPC coefficients; librosa lpc synthesis in speech processing | not: prediction-error-filter (the FIR analysis filter with transfer function A(z), not G/A(z)); linear-prediction-coefficient (the scalar parameters a_k, not the filter itself) [formal: filter praedictionis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

definition.body: An algebraic code-excited linear prediction (ACELP) codec is a human-made speech coding algorithm that represents the residual excitation signal as a sparse linear combination of codewords from an algebraic codebook, filtered through a linear prediction synthesis filter. Its parameters are: (1) the algebraic codebook structure (fixed codebook with sparse impulse positions, e.g., 4 pulses per subframe), (2) the pitch delay (fixed or adaptive codebook), (3) the gain factors for both codebook and pitch excitation, and (4) the linear prediction analysis order and frame length (typically 20ms frames, 160 samples at 8kHz). It persists in ITU-T G.729, ETSI GSM-EFR, and 3GPP AMR speech codecs, implemented in mobile baseband processors and VoIP software. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 Annex B ACELP codec; ETSI GSM-EFR 13 kbps ACELP; 3GPP AMR narrowband mode; Adobe Flash SoundCodec 3 (Speex) uses ACELP variant | not: speech-codec (broader class including MP3, AAC, OPUS); linear-prediction-filter (the synthesis filter component, not the full ACELP algorithm) [formal: codex excitationis algebraicae praedictionis linearis | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
